overview: The Nimiipuu, commonly called Nez Perce, built influential networks of villages, fishing places and travel routes across the interior Pacific Northwest. Their homeland includes parts of present-day Idaho, Oregon and Washington. The two imported outlines are rough regional footprints, and their 1492 and 1500 starting dates do not mark the people’s beginning. Nimiipuu communities continue today.

periods.title: River homelands and wider connections
periods.summary: Fishing, gathering, trade and later mounted travel linked communities across a broad homeland.

periods.title: Treaties and dispossession
periods.summary: United States treaties and incoming settlers reduced landholding; several bands rejected the 1863 agreement.

periods.title: Flight and exile
periods.summary: War scattered families into captivity and Canada; survivors later returned to the Northwest.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: Dispersed families maintained relationships, while teaching and restoration programs renewed cultural practices.

sections.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes

items.text: Leaders did not all have the same job. The Tribe’s history describes separate expertise in fishing, hunting, warfare and religion, with councils guiding decisions. Knowledge and skill mattered when communities chose leaders. Political life grew from the work people needed to do together.

River benches provided level places for villages. People caught salmon through much of the warmer season and dried fish for winter. Canoes made by burning and chipping logs connected settlements and trading partners. A river could serve as pantry, road and meeting place at once.

Horses reached Nez Perce communities in the early eighteenth century and expanded travel for hunting, including journeys for bison. This added new possibilities to an older river-based economy. The canoe did not suddenly become useless when someone acquired a horse.

Camas gathering rewarded patience: leaving small bulbs underground helped provide another harvest. At Weippe Prairie in September 1805, visiting expedition members saw families digging, cleaning and preparing bulbs. Earthen kilns cooked the food, which could then become bread and other meals.

Expedition member Patrick Gass thought camas bread tasted rather like pumpkin bread. The guests kept accepting so much food that Nez Perce leaders eventually asked them to pay for more. Hospitality had limits, even for travelers with a very large appetite.

Tule stems contain spongy, air-filled tissue. Woven into mats, they insulated homes, swelled in wet weather to keep rain out, and shrank in dry weather to allow ventilation. Lightweight mats could be rolled up for moving camp: the walls could travel with the household.

The same mat-making skills furnished sleeping surfaces, room dividers and places to dry food. Sedges supplied cordage with little preparation beyond drying. Such plant technologies turned riverbank materials into a whole household toolkit, including ways to organize space and preserve the harvest.

A cradleboard in the park museum, dated about 1900, combines a wooden support, soft buckskin and a velveteen hood. Its label describes grandmothers, mothers, aunts and older sisters carrying children. This object makes family care visible alongside the better-known stories of chiefs and battles.

Gold discovered inside the reservation in 1860 brought newcomers onto protected land. The 1863 treaty proposed a drastic reduction of the reservation. Bands whose homes lay outside the new boundary refused to sign. The United States nevertheless ratified the document, creating a dangerous gap between its demands and those communities’ consent.

In 1877, several non-treaty bands fled the United States Army with families and horses. Their journey lasted 126 days and covered more than 1,170 miles. The attack at Big Hole killed children and other civilians as well as warriors. The final siege at Bear Paw ended in October.

Some families escaped into Canada; others were sent through Kansas into Indian Territory. In 1885, survivors were finally allowed back to the Northwest, but Joseph’s band was placed on the Colville Reservation rather than returned to Wallowa. Exile separated relatives long after the fighting ended.

sections.title: Teaching, writing and bringing fish back

items.text: Ida Blackeagle learned cornhusk weaving at twelve and later taught at Lapwai High School. In 1966, she and Viola Morris became park cultural demonstrators. Their teaching carried craft knowledge between generations. Cornhusks themselves had become an important substitute when nineteenth-century restrictions limited access to older basket materials.

The Tribe’s language page prints “’íin ’eekíce poxpok’láana” with the translation “I see a ball”. This modern teaching sentence uses a spelling system approved by an advisory board of Elders. The page explains that ordinary Nimipuutimt sentences use lowercase letters, so the small initial letter is intentional.

In 1994, the Tribe obtained coho salmon eggs that otherwise faced disposal and began a restoration effort. Tribal fisheries staff raised and released young fish to rebuild a vanished run. A tribal commission account explains how biological work depended on treaty rights, negotiations and funding as well as hatchery tanks.

ending.text: The imported map cutoffs do not end Nimiipuu history. The 1877 war and exile transformed lives, but communities continue in Idaho, Washington, Oregon, Canada and elsewhere, connected by family relationships and cultural work.
